processing: Spring leaf processed as black tea, as with other Assam orthodox or CTC production; the seasonal leaf, not a special method, sets it apart.
harvest_season: Spring: from March, with one account giving mid-March to early May. It is followed by the more prized second flush in May and June.
appearance_dry: Dark leaf from young growth, as is typical of spring black tea; no fuller description is documented.
appearance_liquor: Golden yellow, lighter than a second flush.
appearance_wet: Soft young leaf, as is typical of spring growth.
taste_profile: Lighter and fresher than classic Assam, fragrant and flowery with subtle floral notes, and usually a little spicier than its Darjeeling equivalent.

brewing.notes: Try it plain first. It is a lighter tea than a second flush, so strong milk may bury it.

vintage_note: Usually best bought by harvest year and estate, and drunk fresh, as is typical of spring teas.
description:
Assam first flush is the spring picking from the Brahmaputra Valley, the first growth after the bushes rest for the winter. It is the Assam for people who think they know Assam: lighter, fresher, less of a breakfast hammer.

The leaf is young and tender, and estates process it as black tea in the normal way. What changes the cup is the season, not a special method.

Expect floral lift and spring freshness, with a little more spice than a Darjeeling picked at the same time. Most people go wrong by treating it like a CTC, brewing it hard with milk, and losing what makes it worth buying.

Look for the estate name, the year and the flush on the pack. The region's reputation rests on the second flush, so compare the two side by side: that tells you more than any description.
history: Little is documented specifically about first flush as a style. It takes its name from the seasonal rhythm of Indian tea, and it stands behind the May and June second flush, considered the best quality in Assam.
